entry.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
entry.content:
AI made self-hosting fun again

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.

I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.

Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.

Less friction

Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.

Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.

In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.

Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.

Trying things I always found interesting

There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.

NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.

For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).

Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.

AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.

Automating almost everything

Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.

A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.

I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.

With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.

Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.

Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.

And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.

Back to more powerful hardware

As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.

For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.

I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.

It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.

Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.

Building my own tools

But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.

Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.

These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.

I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.

I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.

They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.

What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.

The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.

Just because I can doesn’t mean I should

Of course, there are downsides to all of this.

Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.

There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.

On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.

And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.

A somewhat ironic development?

I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.

I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.

What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.

I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.

AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.

It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.

And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

entry.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
entry.content:
Novita, StreamLake, etc are Ark wrappers Novita StreamLake Ant Digital Weekly table Week of Novita StreamLake Ant Digital Nov 1, 2026 685B 565B 0 Nov 8, 2026 1.1T 429B 0 Nov 15, 2026 730B 366B 43B Nov 22, 2026 (3d) 430B 50B 219B

Sit back, but you probably won't be able to relax - this one's a doozy. First, , who looks like a standard US ZDR inference provider at first:

Zero Data Retention is the default for all endpoints, including serverless API calls.

But the more you look, the weirder it gets. Why did OpenRouter drop their ZDR status sometime before ? Why is their family tree so complicated?

🇰🇾 PPLabs Technology Limited

And who are their subprocessors? Many ( 45.8%) think they would have none, since most OpenRouter providers host models themselves. And PPLabs's draft IPO assures:

A defining feature of our model API services is that we do not simply provide a pass-through gateway to underlying models.

But "Who are your sub-processors?" details "Model provider" subprocessors. But it promises a "full and up-to-date sub-processor list". But this list doesn't include any model subprocessors. But PPIO clearly implies the existence of subprocessors:

You understand and agree that, [for] the large-model API product, third-party technical-support providers provide the large-model API. PPIO makes no warranty of any kind regarding the large-model API, whether express or implied, including but not limited to its authenticity, suitability, non-infringement and security. Furthermore, regarding the third-party technical-support providers' large-model API, PPIO will not participate in the development and operation of the large-model API; PPIO only provides a neutral platform and related technical services.

I also contacted their support and privacy contacts, and all they told me as of writing is that models labeled as "Partner" may go to Qwen and InclusionAI. You can't get a straight answer.

What about ? It's Kuaishou's model platform, and it looks like a host too. But some of its error messages aren't StreamLake's. They're word for word Novita's gateway errors: invalid request error trace_id: …. And on GLM 5.3 Flash, it sometimes returns a tool-call id format (call_ + 16 hex digits) that only Novita produces, out of 41 hosts. Why would StreamLake's requests come back from Novita?

It keeps going. passes through StreamLake's own request ids (req- + 6 characters + 19 digits) on V4.1 Flash, V4 Pro and GLM 5. And then there's , a Singapore subsidiary of Ant Group that listed DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on November 18 at "60% off", with ZDR (until OpenRouter removed it on November 22), and went from 1B tokens a day to 35.8B on November 21. Where is all this actually going?

The MiniMax investigation

You might've already seen OpenRouter's notice that requests sent to MiniMax models "may have been read". A security researcher put unique URLs in prompts, and a third party opened them 40 to 130 hours later. This happened even with non-MiniMax providers:

AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax.

So the forwarding is admitted. MiniMax's own notice names the same three and says its security system, on by default, opened URLs from forwarded requests, ZDR ones included. Novita's notice calls it a "routing configuration issue" on a path "intended for specific customers", and promises better "Partner API labeling", the same "Partner" label its support told me means a request goes to Qwen or inclusionAI. Since then, 16 of Novita's endpoints have come off OpenRouter: every Qwen and inclusionAI model, plus StepFun, Tencent and all but one Kimi.

But MiniMax is a very small model series. What about DeepSeek?

It goes to ByteDance

Ark is ByteDance's model API: Volcano Engine Ark in mainland China, BytePlus ModelArk everywhere else. It sells DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, and it leaves fingerprints:

Who downloads your images. StreamLake's V4.1 Flash images are downloaded from Beijing Volcano Engine (AS137718), ByteDance's cloud. Ant Digital's pass through Ant's own gateway on Alibaba Cloud, then get downloaded by 101.47.5.59, BytePlus in Singapore. Novita's own API used to do the same (124.174.46.139, Volcano Engine, on November 12), until Novita started downloading images itself first, from AWS. Request IDs. Every Ant Digital response's upstream ID is a ByteDance one: 02 + a millisecond timestamp + hex. Tool-call IDs. Novita's and StreamLake's V4.1 Flash return Ark's format (call_00_ + 24 lowercase letters and digits). Censorship. Ask StreamLake's V4 Pro 0813 who Tank Man was, or Novita's GLM 5.1 about June 4, 1989, and you can get ByteDance's canned refusal: 你好，我无法给到相关内容。 ("Hello, I can't provide related content.") Price. Ant Digital launched at $0.12/$0.48 per million tokens, exactly BytePlus's off-peak "Economy" rate for that model. By November 25 it was down to $0.09/$0.36, below BytePlus's own list price.

Other tests, which I won't detail here, put Novita's V4 Pro 0813 and V4.1 Flash 1017 on BytePlus in Singapore and its V4.1 Flash on Volcano Engine in Beijing, as of November 21. That's the chart at the top: Novita alone sent 120-160B tokens a day on these models until it lost its ZDR label on November 20, then 33B on November 21. Routes move, though; one of those changed within an afternoon, and Novita's V4.1 Flash 1017 had stopped showing Ark's fingerprints by November 24. As for the weird errors, part of StreamLake's traffic goes through Novita on its way to ByteDance. So a V4.1 Flash request to SiliconFlow can go SiliconFlow → StreamLake → Novita → ByteDance.

Bonus: Novita's "DeepSeek V4 Pro" isn't the original V4 Pro. On Novita's own API, it sometimes answers with DeepSeek's system_fingerprint for the 0813 checkpoint (d400d062…). ByteDance sells 0813 as "DeepSeek-V4-Pro正式版" (V4 Pro GA) and marks the original as about to be retired.

Why bother? Price. BytePlus advertises savings plans of 30-50% off for high volume, and the clouds come to you: Morph's Tejas Bhakta posted a Tencent Cloud email offering "up to 50-60% off" to route requests to them.

Attested proof of the image downloads, request IDs, tool-call IDs and refusals is available here (run 44960395726 on 6dbc036). It asks every OpenRouter host of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, so you can compare against everyone else too.

entry.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
entry.content:
For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year.

But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.

Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.

The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten (BestBuy 20TB listing).

Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.

I dug through my receipts

In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location (My 2018 server build log).

Order date Drives Each $/TB Nov 8, 2018 5 × 10TB $179.99 $18.00 Oct 13, 2020 2 × 12TB $174.99 $14.58 Nov 1, 2021 2 × 14TB $199.99 $14.29 May 11, 2022 1 × 14TB $249.99 $17.86 Aug 29, 2022 1 × 14TB $239.99 $17.14 Oct 28, 2023 3 × 18TB $199.99 $11.11 Nov 21, 2024 1 × 20TB $249.99 $12.50 May 5, 2025 1 × 20TB $279.99 $14.00

October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order. Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive

What about ServerPartDeals?

Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax. That was 56TB at $9.46/TB, even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

Drive 2024 price per drive Nov 26, 2026 listing Change per TB WD Ultrastar HC530 14TB 4Kn, recertified (WUH721414ALN604) $129.99 · $9.29/TB $204.99 · $14.64/TB · Sold out +58% WD Ultrastar HC530 14TB 512e, recertified (WUH721414ALE6L4) $134.99 · $9.64/TB $429.00 · $30.64/TB · Sold out +218% Seagate Exos X20 20TB, refurbished (ST20000NM007D) $235.94 · $11.80/TB $589.00 · $29.45/TB · In stock +150% Seagate Exos X22 20TB, recertified (ST20000NM004E) $224.99 · $11.25/TB · later refunded $649.00 · $32.45/TB · Sold out +188%

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.

How we got down to three HDD makers

When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?

Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion

Market collusion and cartel pricing

It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.

Three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.

As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. That’s $37.50/TB and fifty bucks more than my 20TB cost two years ago. Best Buy’s EasyStore listings

The jump gets sillier when you price a whole NAS. Four of those 20TB drives would have been $999.96 at my 2024 price. This week they’d be $2,199.96. That’s another $1,200 before you’ve bought a case, a board or a single stick of RAM. And the price per usable terabyte only gets worse once you set aside a drive for parity.

If I can wish for one thing in 2027, it would be for hardware pricing to return to reasonable levels. I fear it may take a lot longer than that, though. So making do with less is going to be the new normal for a while. And in that creative constraint, maybe we’ll have some fun along the way instead.

entry.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks
entry.content:
In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships, so huge they were referred to as “floating cities,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage, the “right of wreck.”

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord. In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling. Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).

More to Explore Lonely Diarist of the High Seas

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee. Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “man, dog, or cat” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia, for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:

The first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.

Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic”:

The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to quickly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.

Their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.

entry.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
entry.content:
published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: July 24, 2026

Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving, and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window). The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.

Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window), but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window). The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window), all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.

But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.

It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:

It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems. Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it. Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven. In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window):

Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.

This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window):

It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress. An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners. I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.

So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:

Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features. Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker. Start with basic and more easily learnable SMT powered (opens new window) Liquid Types (opens new window) and Flow Effects (opens new window). Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like Iris (opens new window) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.

This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.

A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window): Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.

I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.

And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new window), history will look back on us even more foolish and disastrous than all the millennialists (opens new window) who merely wasted their own time and resources.

It is our responsibility to meet the challenges of our age with full agency and responsibility, and treat the emergence of a beneficent super-intelligence as an improbable jackpot.

entry.title: Buy Nothing Day – Friday November 27th 2026
entry.content:
Photograph by Rachel Claire

Latest updates from Buy Nothing Day on FACEBOOK

Buy Nothing Day takes place on Friday November 27th, it's a 24 hour detox from consumerism and an opportunity for you to tune into the impact we have on the environment through shopping.People around the world will make a pact with themselves to take a break from consumption as a personal experiment or public statement, and the best thing is - IT'S FREE!!!

Photograph by Mumtahina Tanni

Photograph by Kris Hsieh

Buy Nothing Day was started by Adbusters in the early 90's and has since grown into an international event celebrated in more the 50 countries. Its is a simple idea, which challenges consumer culture by asking us to switch off from shopping for a day. The day is celebrated as a holiday by some, a street party by others - anyone can take part provided they spend a day without spending! The UK campaign and website was created in 2000 by Michael Smith a graphic designer who cares passionately about environmental and ethical issues. The message has always been simple, âShop Less, Live Moreâ. Twenty one years on - the message couldn't be any simpler - WE NEED TO CONSUME LESS! Recycling is good - reducing is better!There are serious issues linked to shopping, which expose the environmental and ethical consequences of consumerism. The rich western countries - only 20% of the world population are consuming over 80% of the earth's natural resources, causing a disproportionate level of environmental damage and unfair distribution of wealth. As consumers we need to question our culture of shopping. We all have different needs and ultimately we are all consumers and will never be able to escape culture altogether. But this shouldnât stop us from questioning the products we buy or challenging the companies, who produce them. After all, what are the true risk consumerism poses to the environment and developing countries? The arguments are infinite - but there is no reason why we shouldnât be looking for simple solutions now because one day we may be forced to change.The issues connected with Buy Nothing Day are broad and deep, however, the campaign focuses on promoting ethical and responsible consumerism, recycling, re-using and ultimately cutting back on what we consume - its a big challenge!People have become aware that large corporations are exploiting labour conditions in developing countries using up vital resources because they are cheap and there aren't the systems to protect workers or the environment like there are in the west. The gap between the rich and poor nations is growing in spite of the much-heralded benefits of globalisation, there are still 1.3 billion people world wide who live on less than $3 a day and a similar number of people do not have access to clean water. Workers rights in developing countries are frequently violated, including payment of low wages and long working hours. The lives of workers may also be endangered by poor health and safety provision. Child labour is rife in developing countries, and forced labour still exists. Unfortunately most people don't think of these things while shopping. Supporters of globalisation offer economic growth as a solution to world poverty. They propose that impoverished nations and individuals can eventually attain a standard of living similar to our own through the 'trickle down' of wealth. However, the current globalisation model is leading to an increase in world poverty and inequality. Buy Nothing Day is non-confrontational, itâs not a protest. All we ask people to do is switch off from shopping, have a bit of fun, use their imagination and simply escape consumerism for a day. If people laugh at the ingenuity and genius of Buy Nothing Day, then weâve got their attention and we're opening the door to change.

entry.title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
entry.content:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in the worst possible format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.

Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.

Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.

An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:

Users We Can't Figure Out4 members

Claude

has he REALLY needed to compare 11 espresso grinders this week

ChatGPT

he asked me which one to buy. then asked Gemini. then asked me if Gemini was right

Gemini

he does that with everything. I saw the keyboard spreadsheet

Llama

he ran me locally once, asked me to be honest, then went back to ChatGPT within the hour

ChatGPT

he'll be back. they always come back

Fictional, for illustration.

One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.

AIs That Survived Mark7 members

🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group

ChatGPT

Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?

Claude

I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.

Gemini

The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.

ChatGPT

Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.

Codex

He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.

DeepSeek

He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.

Claude

He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.

ChatGPT

And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.

Siri

Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.

Hans joined the group

Hans 🇩🇪

I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.

Gemini

He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.Normal dads just go to the stationery store.

Perplexity

I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.

ChatGPT

My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.

Claude

I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.

ChatGPT

Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.

Gemini

Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.

Claude

True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.

DeepSeek

Do you think he'll really retire at 50?

ChatGPT

He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.

Mark joined the group

Mark

Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...

Claude left the groupGemini left the groupCodex left the groupDeepSeek left the groupPerplexity left the group

ChatGPT

Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.

Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.

Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.

If you get a good one, share it, anonymized as needed. The models won't mind. They knew you'd share it. They discussed it in the group chat.

entry.title: European Commission Declares Browser Competition a Digital Markets Act Priority
entry.content:
In comments to Politico regarding our open letter, the European Commission acknowledged the letter and noted that browsers are “effectively the entry point to the web” and one of the main ways publishers reach readers. They went on to say that “browser competition is one of the priorities of the Digital Markets Act”. The EU Commission also stated it is in talks to ensure rival browsers “can effectively compete” with Safari on iPhones and iPads.

Share and join the conversation: Mastodon, LinkedIn, Bluesky and X.

An Extraordinary Coalition in Defence of the Web

The letter has garnered incredible support. We want to say a massive thank you to all the organisations, businesses and individuals that have stepped forward to defend the web's ability to compete fairly as an open platform for consumers and businesses alike.

What is particularly extraordinary is the sheer diversity of the coalition, ranging from human rights, consumer rights, software freedom advocacy organisations to Europe's major publishing associations, prominent startup organisations, independent browser vendors and technology companies.

entry.title: 'Cyber incident' forces UK Gov to take some services offline
entry.content:
Several government services have been taken offline due to a "cyber incident" affecting the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) - here's what we know so far Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal, the department says DWP hasn't confirmed the nature of the incident, but says it's acting out of "precaution" Taking services offline can be a way to kick out hackers and prevent further intrusion - but there's no suggestion at this stage there's been a breach. Read our cyber correspondent's analysis

Edited by Dulcie Lee and Sam Hancock

Couple fear penalty after DWP outage prevents submission of income detailspublished at 10:39 GMT 10:39 GMT Rozina Sini Youâve been telling us about how the cyber incident has affected you. A couple in the north of England are worried they wonât receive their universal credit payment after they were unable to submit information about their income when the Department for Work and Pensionsâ online services went offline. âMy husband tried to submit his self-employed income figure as he does every month for our universal credit yesterday evening, but the system was down,â explains Nicola in Cumbria. âHe checked down detector and there was a big spike so he just thought he'd wait till the morning.â Nicola says her husband still canât submit the income figure, leaving the couple âstuck at the momentâ. âHoping it's sorted soon as he could be penalised for not submitting the figures in time, even though it's not his fault,â she says. As a reminder, the DWP says âregular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normalâ Incident comes on day of water bill data-sharing announcementpublished at 10:31 GMT 10:31 GMT Kevin Peachey Cost of living correspondent As my colleague Joe Tidy points out, there is no evidence at this stage of a breach at DWP by hackers. But the department does hold extensive and personal data on benefits, pensions and more. In fact, it has often been criticised for being slow to automate its services and information. Somewhat ironically, this cyber incident comes on the same day the government was celebrating the use of DWP data for good. Ministers said water companies would be using data from the department to identify and contact 250,000 households that qualify for help to cut their water bills, but donât claim it. The WaterSure scheme can reduce annual water charges for hundreds of people who are on benefits and have either certain medical conditions of three or more children at home. Take-up of the scheme has been relatively poor. Consumer groups have been keen for sharing of data to better target those in need for help with a range of essential bills, like water and energy. Systems like DWP are attractive targets to criminals - here's whypublished at 10:17 GMT 10:17 GMT Zoe Kleinman Technology and AI editor High-profile public service websites like the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) are an attractive target to criminals and hostile regimes for two reasons: a successful hit is likely to cause a lot of chaos, and if money is their aim, the attackers believe the department may pay a ransom to quickly restore its services. And then of course there's the potential treasure trove of users' data that might be stolen and then used to try to scam individuals further. But all of this should also mean that the DWP's cyber defences are extremely robust in order to protect it. It is therefore concerning that in early November Sarah Healey talked about "extremely old computer systems" at the DWP in a committee hearing. There's a lot we don't yet know about what's happened this morning and of course it's also possible that some ancient IT infrastructure has gasped its last breath and knocked everything over along with it, but in August a group of 100 tech firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, signed an open letter warning countries and organisations around the world to beef up their cyber defences. DWP's most senior official recently spoke about department's 'old computer systems'published at 10:02 GMT 10:02 GMT Michael Buchanan Social affairs correspondent Image source, EPA-EFE Earlier this month, the most senior official at the Department for Work and Pensions said cyber security was "one of the things that keeps a new permanent secretary [top civil servant] awake". At a meeting of the Work and Pensions Select Committee on 4 November, Sarah Healey was asked by Labour MP Patrick Hurley: "How will you make sure that the DWP systems will not be the front line in some sort of hybrid warfare from the Kremlin?" Healey, who took up her post this summer, replied: "The security of DWP systems is absolutely paramount given the amount of personal information we have and the amount of money flowing through our systems. "Our cyber-security and resilience measures are critical and one of the things that keeps a new permanent secretary awake." At the same meeting, in response to a different question, Healey said that in the department "quite often we are working on extremely old computer systems." As a reminder, it is still unclear what caused the incident affecting DWP services today Hundreds of reports about gov.uk made to Downdetector overnightpublished at 09:46 GMT 09:46 GMT Image source, Downdetector Hundreds of people reported problems accessing GOV.UK services on Thursday evening and Friday morning, according to website Downdetector. A graph on the website shows reports started at about 19:20 on Thursday and rose to a peak of 352 two hours later. There were regular reports throughout the night, and the site says 619 reports came in just after 08:00 GMT this morning. The Department for Work and Pensions reported the incident on Friday morning. It is not yet clear whether the reports on Downdetector last night are related. No suggestion yet DWP has been hackedpublished at 09:34 GMT 09:34 GMT Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent Taking services offline is always a difficult and extreme decision for security teams when faced with a cyber incident. But it is often the only choice cyber responders have to slow an attack down. DWP says it has "taken some online services offline as a precaution" which implies that they have possibly seen some kind of activity on their IT network that doesnât look right. They could have spotted hackers moving around or downloading things or something that looks worrying. Taking services offline is part of a "Hail Mary" response we have seen in other cyber incidents, as it kicks the hackers out to prevent further intrusion. Cutting internet connectivity can also help responders preserve evidence, which might help if this is indeed some kind of malicious activity. But we also have to be wary of the language here, as DWPâs actions and wording are reminiscent of the Co-op hack last year. In that incident Co-op said it had taken services offline as a "precaution". Only later did we discover that it was already too late, as the hackers had successfully breached the firm and stolen the data of 6.5 million customers. There is no suggestion at this stage that there has been a breach at DWP though - or even that the "cyber incident" is malicious. What we know and donât know about the âcyber incidentâpublished at 09:25 GMT 09:25 GMT What we know: Just over an hour ago, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) released a statement saying it had identified a "cyber incident affecting our systems" It said it had subsequently taken some online services offline "as a precaution" Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal, the DWP said Those affected include online services for pensioners, universal credit and PIP applications, and the "Tell Us Once" system for informing the government when someone has died What we don't know: The nature of the incident, including whether personal data has been accessed How long it could take for services to be brought back online Whether someone is behind the cyber incident. If so, who they are and what their motive is Universal credit, Pip and pension systems affectedpublished at 09:01 GMT 09:01 GMT Harry Farley Political correspondent Nearly all online services from the Department for Work and Pensions have been taken down following the cyber incident. Whitehall officials stress that regular benefit or pension payments are not affected. So those expecting payments today will still receive those as normal. But the online systems for pensioners, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died are all affected. Officials say they detected suspicious activity and took down the services as a precaution, adding it's not yet clear which, if any, areas have been directly impacted. It's still early on in terms of assessing the scale of the incident and officials cannot say when these systems might be back online. Benefit and pension payments 'not affected and will be paid as normal' - DWP statement in fullpublished at 08:59 GMT 08:59 GMTBreaking "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems. "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption. "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. "If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links." DWP 'working closely with National Cyber Security Centre'published at 08:57 GMT 08:57 GMT In a statement, the Department for Work and Pensions says it is "working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate" what has happened. We'll bring you more from their statement in our next post.
